definition: Laudatory means expressing praise and admiration.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word laudatory. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know laudatory should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The retirement toast was so laudatory that the modest coach kept checking whether someone famous had walked in behind him.
A favorable review leans positive but may still note flaws; it stops short of laudatory, which is praise through and through.
Gushing goes further than laudatory, into excess — praise so unmeasured it starts to embarrass everyone, including its subject.

Admiring means showing warm, genuine approval — a tone as much as a judgment, and you can be admiring in complete silence. Laudatory describes the language itself: words whose whole business is praise, as in a laudatory review or citation. Admiring is the feeling; laudatory is the wording.

Complimentary remarks offer compliments, sometimes only out of politeness — a host calling every dish delicious. Laudatory language goes further and means it: praise is its whole purpose, not social smoothing. A complimentary aside flatters the moment; a laudatory citation honors a record.

Approving signals agreement or acceptance, and it runs cooler than praise — a nod, a signed-off report. Laudatory language does not merely accept; it admires out loud. A committee can be approving without one warm word, while a laudatory introduction is warm from first line to last.

so harshly critical it shrivels its target

The yearbook's page on the drama club was purely laudatory — every production 'triumphant,' every set 'ingenious' — and the faculty adviser cut only one adjective, for space.
Laudatory describes language whose whole business is praise.
It is stronger than 'favorable': a favorable report may note flaws along the way, but a laudatory one exists to admire.

Laudatory is a reviewer's and reporter's word — apply it to the words of praise (a laudatory review, citation, introduction), not to the praiseworthy thing itself; that is 'laudable.' Keep it apart from this unit's toady, too: laudatory praise can be entirely sincere, while a toady's flattery is praise with an angle.

When the county magazine assigned a profile of the retiring bridge engineer, the editor expected a few dry paragraphs about load limits.
What came back was frankly laudatory: forty years of flawless inspections recounted like a saga, with whole sentences given over to praise of her judgment.
The editor hesitated — the magazine prided itself on restraint — but the fact-checkers came back with nothing overstated.
Every bridge she had certified still stood, and the one she had condemned failed within the year, empty, exactly as she had warned.
The profile ran unchanged, and readers wrote in to say the praise had, if anything, been too mild.
